expectedText:
SALE-OF-BUSINESS AND DISSOLUTION NONCOMPETE EXCEPTIONS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp. · Jane Doe

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet states California's statutory exceptions to the general rule voiding noncompete restraints, as those exceptions apply to (1) a sale of the goodwill or ownership interests of Acme Corp., and (2) a partner's or member's departure from Acme Corp. by dissolution or dissociation. It states the statute's own conditions for each exception — who qualifies, and what limits apply to the resulting restriction. It is not advice about whether any specific proposed noncompete restriction actually satisfies those conditions for Acme Corp.

THESE ARE EXCEPTIONS TO A GENERAL BAN
California's default rule voids, to that extent, every contract restraining anyone from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business. The sale-of-goodwill exception and the partnership/LLC dissolution-or-dissociation exceptions described in this information sheet are exceptions to that general rule, not a separate freestanding source of authority to restrain competition — a restriction that doesn't satisfy one of the statute's own exceptions remains void under the general rule.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, general rule voiding restraints on lawful business (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16600.)
  Known gap: This clause cites the general voiding rule only for framing — it is a single subdivision of Business and Professions Code Section 16600 and does not itself state the sale-of-business or partnership/LLC dissolution exceptions, which are separate sections addressed in the other clauses of this information sheet. Section 16600 also has a subdivision (b) (an employment-context reading rule) and a subdivision (c) (extending the rule to restraints on non-parties) that are not addressed here because they concern the general employment-noncompete rule covered by this project's separate Non-Compete Agreement document, not the sale-of-business or dissolution exceptions that are this document's subject.

THE SALE-OF-GOODWILL EXCEPTION
California law permits a noncompete agreement in three specific sale-of-business situations: (1) a person sells the goodwill of a business; (2) an owner of a business entity sells or otherwise disposes of all of that owner's ownership interest in the entity; or (3) an owner of a business entity sells all or substantially all of the entity's operating assets together with its goodwill (or the operating assets of a division or subsidiary together with that division's or subsidiary's goodwill, or all of a subsidiary's ownership interest). In any of those situations, the seller may agree with the buyer not to carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area in which the business, division, or subsidiary being sold has been carried on — but only for so long as the buyer, or anyone who derives title to the goodwill or ownership interest from the buyer, itself carries on a like business there.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any person who sells the goodwill of a business, or any owner of a business entity selling or otherwise disposing of all of his or her ownership interest in the business entity, or any owner of a business entity that sells (a) all or substantially all of its operating assets together with the goodwill of the business entity, (b) all or substantially all of the operating assets of a division or a subsidiary of the business entity together with the goodwill of that division or subsidiary, or (c) all of the ownership interest of any subsidiary, may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business within a specified geographic area in which the business so sold, or that of the business entity, division, or subsidiary has been carried on, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the goodwill or ownership interest from the buyer, carries on a like business therein."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (first paragraph), California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill/ownership-interest/asset-sale exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16601.)
  Known gap: This is a single, continuous statutory sentence — the (a)/(b)/(c) markers quoted below are the statute's own internal list of the asset-sale scenarios within that one sentence, not separate numbered subdivisions of Section 16601 (Section 16601 has no lettered subdivisions at its top level; a companion clause quotes its separately paragraphed definitions). The restriction's validity is conditioned on the buyer's continued operation: the statute ties the seller's restraint to the buyer (or a successor in title to the goodwill or ownership interest) actually carrying on a like business in the specified area, not to a fixed time period — this document does not address what happens if the buyer stops operating the business, which the statute's text does not itself resolve. "Specified geographic area" is not defined further by this section, and the statute does not itself require the area to match the area the business previously served, only that it be an area in which the business, division, or subsidiary sold has been carried on.

WHO COUNTS AS A COVERED SELLER
Section 16601 defines its own key terms, and those definitions control who can use the sale-of-goodwill exception. A “business entity” means a partnership (including a limited partnership or limited liability partnership), a limited liability company (including a series LLC), or a corporation. An “owner of a business entity” means a partner (for a partnership), a member (for an LLC), or a stockholder (for a corporation). An “ownership interest” means, correspondingly, a partnership interest, a membership interest, or (the statute's own, non-parallel wording) “a capital stockholder” in the case of a corporation. A “subsidiary” means a business entity over which the selling business entity has voting control, a right to receive a majority share of liquidating distributions, or both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "For the purposes of this section, “business entity” means any partnership (including a limited partnership or a limited liability partnership), limited liability company (including a series of a limited liability company formed under the laws of a jurisdiction that recognizes such a series), or corporation."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (“business entity” definition), California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill exception, definition of “business entity” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16601.)
  "For the purposes of this section, “owner of a business entity” means any partner, in the case of a business entity that is a partnership (including a limited partnership or a limited liability partnership), or any member, in the case of a business entity that is a limited liability company (including a series of a limited liability company formed under the laws of a jurisdiction that recognizes such a series), or any owner of capital stock, in the case of a business entity that is a corporation."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (“owner of a business entity” definition), California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill exception, definition of “owner of a business entity” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16601.)
  "For the purposes of this section, “ownership interest” means a partnership interest, in the case of a business entity that is a partnership (including a limited partnership a limited liability partnership), a membership interest, in the case of a business entity that is a limited liability company (including a series of a limited liability company formed under the laws of a jurisdiction that recognizes such a series), or a capital stockholder, in the case of a business entity that is a corporation."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (“ownership interest” definition), California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill exception, definition of “ownership interest” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16601.)
  "For the purposes of this section, “subsidiary” means any business entity over which the selling business entity has voting control or from which the selling business entity has a right to receive a majority share of distributions upon dissolution or other liquidation of the business entity (or has both voting control and a right to receive these distributions.)"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (“subsidiary” definition), California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill exception, definition of “subsidiary” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16601.)
  Known gap: All four citations below are separate definitional paragraphs within the same statutory section (§ 16601), not independent sections — no additional independent source was sought or needed for these definitions beyond the statute's own text. One definition is worth flagging as an apparent drafting inconsistency in the statute's own text, not a transcription choice made here: the “ownership interest” definition defines the corporate-context term as “a capital stockholder,” which describes a person, not an interest — inconsistent with the parallel “partnership interest” / “membership interest” phrasing in the same sentence for the other two entity types. That inconsistency is quoted here exactly as it appears in the current codified text, and this document does not attempt to resolve or correct it.

THE PARTNERSHIP DISSOLUTION/DISSOCIATION EXCEPTION
A separate statute permits a noncompete agreement between partners of Acme Corp., tied to the partnership's dissolution or to one partner's dissociation from it. A partner may agree, upon or in anticipation of either a dissolution of the partnership or that partner's own dissociation from it, not to carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area where the partnership business has been transacted — but, as with the sale-of-goodwill exception, only for so long as another partner (or someone who derives title to the business or its goodwill from that other partner) itself carries on a like business there.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Any partner may, upon or in anticipation of any of the circumstances described in subdivision (b), agree that he or she will not carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area where the partnership business has been transacted, so long as any other member of the partnership, or any person deriving title to the business or its goodwill from any such other member of the partnership, carries on a like business therein."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16602(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, partner noncompete on dissolution or dissociation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16602.)
  "(b) Subdivision (a) applies to either of the following circumstances: (1) A dissolution of the partnership. (2) Dissociation of the partner from the partnership."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16602(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, the two circumstances subdivision (a) covers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16602.)
  Known gap: The two citations below are subdivisions (a) and (b) of a single statutory section (§ 16602); no additional independent source was needed for this specific exception beyond the statute's own text. This exception is distinct from, and does not depend on, the sale-of-goodwill exception in § 16601 — a partner can invoke it on dissociation or dissolution without any sale of the business occurring at all. This document does not address the separate statutory definitions of “dissolution” and “dissociation” of a partnership themselves (found elsewhere in the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, not in this section), only the noncompete exception that Section 16602 ties to those two events.

THE LLC DISSOLUTION/TERMINATION-OF-INTEREST EXCEPTION
A parallel statute extends the same kind of exception to members of Acme Corp., if Acme Corp. is a limited liability company (including a series of an LLC formed under the laws of a jurisdiction that recognizes series LLCs). A member may agree, upon or in anticipation of a dissolution of the LLC or the termination of that member's own interest in it, not to carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area where the LLC's business has been transacted — again, only for so long as another member (or someone who derives title to the business or its goodwill from that other member) itself carries on a like business there.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any member may, upon or in anticipation of a dissolution of, or the termination of his or her interest in, a limited liability company (including a series of a limited liability company formed under the laws of a jurisdiction recognizing such a series), agree that he or she or it will not carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area where the limited liability company business has been transacted, so long as any other member of the limited liability company, or any person deriving title to the business or its goodwill from any such other member of the limited liability company, carries on a like business therein."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16602.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, LLC member noncompete on dissolution or termination of interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16602.5.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory sentence with no internal lettered or numbered subdivisions, so only one citation is given below; it is nonetheless one full, independent statutory section (§ 16602.5), not a subdivision of § 16601 or § 16602, though its structure closely parallels § 16602's partnership exception. Unlike § 16602(b), this section does not separately enumerate “termination of interest” the way § 16602 enumerates “dissociation” and “dissolution” as two distinct listed circumstances — it instead names “a dissolution of, or the termination of his or her interest in,” the LLC as a single compound trigger phrase. This document does not address the LLC statute's own separate definitions of dissociation or dissolution (found in the Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, not in this section) beyond what Section 16602.5 itself says.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
The undersigned acknowledge that they have reviewed this statement of California's statutory exceptions to the general noncompete ban — for a sale of Acme Corp.'s goodwill, ownership interests, or operating assets, and for a partner's or member's departure from Acme Corp. by dissolution or dissociation — and understand that whether a specific proposed noncompete restriction actually satisfies a given exception's conditions is a fact-specific question this information sheet does not resolve.

Seller/Partner/Member: Jane Doe
Date: _______________

Buyer/Business: John Smith
Date: _______________
